lead: Every wire is a resistor with a current limit. It carries its load current with a small voltage drop, and it survives a fault current only for a short time before insulation or copper fails. Protection devices—fuses, current limiters, limiting resistors and circuit breakers—break or limit that fault current before the wire is damaged. The device is chosen from the wire's derated rating, not from the load alone. This rule sets feeder sizes, breaker panels and reset actions on every aircraft electrical bus.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for the busbar and feeder arrangement that connects sources to loads.

blocks.text: Aircraft wire uses stranded copper, not solid copper, because vibration and repeated bending crack a solid conductor. Strands are often silver plated for soldering and corrosion resistance, or nickel plated for hot engine and galley areas. Insulation is chosen by temperature and fire behaviour: PVC for cool protected areas, PTFE for high temperature, Kapton for thin lightweight harnesses, and glass braid where abrasion is severe. The gauge is given in AWG (American Wire Gauge). A lower AWG number means a thicker conductor and a higher current rating; 8 AWG is much thicker than 20 AWG.

The bare current rating of a wire is measured in free air. In an aircraft it must be derated for three effects: bundle size (many wires trapped in one loom cannot shed heat), altitude (thin air cools less), and ambient temperature (a hot bay adds heat). A wire that is safe at 60 A alone may be limited to 40 A in a dense hot bundle. Voltage drop is a second limit. Feeder drop is usually held to a few percent of bus voltage, so long runs need thicker wire even when heating is acceptable. The drop for a DC feeder with a return path is V<sub>drop</sub> = I × R<sub>total</sub> and R<sub>total</sub> = 2 × L × r. Here I is load current in A, L is one-way length in m, r is conductor resistance in Ω/m, and the factor 2 counts the return wire.
Wires are marked with circuit identity, clamped at fixed intervals, and bent no tighter than the stated bend radius. Sharp bends crush insulation and strand the copper.

A fuse is a one-shot device: a metal element melts when its inverse time-current curve says the current is too high for too long. At slight overload it takes minutes; at a short-circuit it takes milliseconds. A current limiter is a heavy-current fast-acting fuse used on a generator or main feeder. It clears a large fault before the downstream busbars see the full current. A limiting resistor is a resistor in series with a circuit to hold fault current or switch-on inrush current down. It does not break the circuit; it buys time for the breaker or fuse.

A circuit breaker can be reset. The thermal type uses a bimetallic strip heated by load current; the magnetic type uses a solenoid that pulls open on a high current; the thermal-magnetic type combines both, giving a delay on overload and fast action on short circuit. A trip-free breaker cannot be held closed on a fault: the handle moves but the contacts stay open until the mechanism resets. Remote-controlled breakers let the crew open and close a feeder from the cockpit.

Breakers are preferred in flight because a crew can reset one after a transient. That advantage is also a danger: repeated resetting of a thermal breaker into a real fault overheats the wire. A fuse is used where a one-shot clearance is acceptable and resetting is not wanted.

Protection is a race between two curves. The wire damage curve gives the time a conductor can carry a given current before its insulation or copper is damaged. The device curve gives the time the fuse or breaker takes to open at that current. At every fault current the device must open sooner than the wire is damaged, so on a time-current graph the device curve lies below the wire curve. At the normal load current the device must not open at all, so its curve rises steeply near its rating. The figure shows a 20 A breaker on a wire rated 25 A: at 40 A the breaker clears in 5.0 s while the wire would survive about 31 s; at 80 A the breaker clears in 1.0 s and the wire limit is about 5.2 s.

Selection starts with the load current, then checks the wire's derated rating, then the voltage drop. The breaker rating must not exceed the derated wire rating. If a 40 A load needs a 50 A breaker, the wire must have a derated rating of at least 50 A. A 50 A breaker on a wire rated 40 A protects the load but not the wire.

The fault path matters. A short at the end of a long feeder has enough resistance to reduce fault current, so the breaker may trip slowly. The return path, connectors and contactors add resistance. Coordination also covers the upstream device: the downstream breaker should clear a local fault before the generator current limiter opens. Busbar layouts and bus tie logic belong to 3.11; generator feeder settings belong to 3.1.

examples.question: A 28 V DC feeder carries 40 A for 6 m from the bus to a load. The conductor is 8 AWG copper with a resistance of 2.06 mΩ per metre, and the return path doubles the length. (a) Find the voltage drop as a percentage of 28 V. (b) Find the power lost in the cable. (c) Suggest a breaker rating, stating the wire condition.
steps: One-way length L = 6 m. The return path makes total conductor length L<sub>total</sub> = 2 × 6 = 12 m.
Resistance per metre r = 2.06 mΩ/m = 0.00206 Ω/m. Total R = r × L<sub>total</sub> = 0.00206 × 12 = 0.02472 Ω.
Voltage drop V<sub>drop</sub> = I × R = 40 × 0.02472 = 0.9888 V, about 0.99 V.

Percentage drop = (0.9888 ÷ 28) × 100 = 3.53 %. This is above a 2 % feeder limit, so 8 AWG is marginal for this 6 m, 40 A run. With 6 AWG (1.30 mΩ/m) the drop would be 40 × 12 × 0.00130 = 0.62 V, 2.2 %; with 4 AWG (0.815 mΩ/m) it is 0.39 V, 1.4 %.

Load current is 40 A, so a 50 A breaker is a practical next standard rating, provided the derated wire rating is at least 50 A. If the derated wire rating is only 40 A, the breaker must be 40 A or the wire made thicker.
examples.answer: Voltage drop 0.99 V (3.53 % of 28 V) and cable loss 39.6 W. The drop is above a 2 % feeder limit, so 8 AWG is marginal and 4 AWG meets it (1.4 %). For part (c), a 50 A breaker only if the derated wire rating is at least 50 A.

traps: Choosing a fuse from the load current alone and ignoring the wire's derated rating.
Resetting a tripped thermal breaker again and again instead of finding the fault.
Treating a current limiter as a resettable breaker, or a limiting resistor as a circuit breaker.
Forgetting the return path in voltage drop, or using one-way length when the return doubles it.
Installing a DC fuse or breaker with an AC voltage rating or insufficient interrupting capacity; a DC arc does not self-extinguish at a zero crossing.

quiz.q: What does a lower AWG number mean for an aircraft wire?
quiz.a: A thicker conductor and a higher current rating.

quiz.q: Name three circuit breaker types used in aircraft.
Why is a wire derated for bundle size?
quiz.a: Wires packed together trap heat, so the bundle runs hotter than a single wire in free air.

quiz.q: What does trip-free mean on a circuit breaker?
quiz.a: The contacts open on a fault even if the handle is held closed; it cannot be held closed against a fault.

quiz.q: A 28 V DC load draws 15 A through a total cable resistance of 0.04 Ω. Find the voltage drop and its percentage of 28 V.
A 30 A load is fed by a wire whose derated rating is 25 A. What is wrong, and what must change?
quiz.a: The load current exceeds the wire rating. Use a thicker wire or reduce the load; the breaker must not exceed the derated wire rating.

quiz.q: A wrongly chosen breaker takes 10 s to trip at 60 A, but the wire it guards is damaged after 8 s at 60 A. (This is a different pair from the figure.) What happens on a 60 A fault, and what must change?
quiz.a: The breaker is slower than the wire, so the insulation is damaged before the breaker clears: the wire becomes the fuse. Fit a lower-rated or faster breaker (like the figure's 20 A breaker, 1.9 s at 60 A) or a thicker wire whose damage time is longer.

quiz.q: Why can a long feeder reduce fault current and delay breaker tripping?
quiz.a: Cable resistance adds to the fault loop, so fault current is lower. On an inverse time-current curve a lower current gives a longer trip time; check an end-of-line fault.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern aircraft move toward solid-state power controllers and arc-fault circuit interrupters, which detect the signature of a series or parallel arc rather than only overcurrent. High-voltage DC systems on more-electric aircraft make DC arc interruption harder because the arc does not self-extinguish at a zero crossing. Research searches: arc fault detection in aviation wiring, solid-state circuit breaker for 270 V DC, and wire insulation ageing under thermal cycling.

figure.caption: A 20 A breaker on a wire rated 25 A, on a log time scale. The breaker curve lies below the wire damage curve at every current: at 40 A it trips in 5.0 s against 30.8 s for the wire, at 80 A in 1.0 s against 5.2 s. Near 20 A it never trips, so normal load does not open it.

spec.aria: Graph of time on a logarithmic scale from 0.1 to 1000 seconds against current from 20 to 100 amps. The breaker curve rises steeply near 20 amps and stays below the wire damage curve, which rises near 25 amps. Marked points: at 40 amps 5 seconds and 30.8 seconds, at 80 amps 1 second and 5.2 seconds.
